summary: Examines how hop-by-hop forwarding, route aggregation and route filtering affect the idea of validating a BGP AS path. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When a route announcement travels from network to network, can you trust the list of stops? This explains why that is hard to check.

subtitle: Understanding the limits of validating BGP routing announcements

tldr.problem: BGP routers receive routing announcements with AS paths claiming to show the route through the network. The question is whether these paths are actually valid and whether traffic will follow them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5123 examines four questions about path validation: whether the originating AS is authorized, whether the path is valid, whether the advertisement is authorized, and whether traffic will actually follow the advertised path. It explores these through detailed examples.
tldr.outcome: The RFC demonstrates that forwarding consistency (traffic actually following the advertised path) cannot be guaranteed, and that route, destination, and transit authorization are deeply intertwined in routing systems in ways that create practical limitations on validation.

today: RFC 5123 remains an important informational document on the fundamental challenges of validating BGP AS paths. It is not obsoleted and provides context for understanding why BGP security mechanisms must operate at other layers rather than relying solely on AS path validation.

sections.title: Path Validation in BGP
sections.content:
When routers exchange routing information using BGP, each announcement includes an AS Path: a list of Autonomous System numbers that the route announcement has traversed. A BGP speaker receiving this information might want to ask: Is this path valid? Can I trust it? Will traffic forwarded along this path actually follow the route that was advertised?

RFC 5123 is an informational document that explores these questions. It examines the challenges of validating the AS path in a BGP routing system, considering how real networks operate with hop-by-hop forwarding, route aggregation, and route filtering. The document does not propose solutions; instead, it establishes why the problem is deeper than it initially appears.
sections.eli5: Imagine asking a messenger: 'Did you really take this route through all these towns?' The RFC shows that there is no simple way to verify their answer, especially when routes get combined or changed along the way.

sections.title: Four Core Questions About Paths
sections.content:
The RFC begins by identifying four fundamental questions a BGP speaker might ask when receiving a routing announcement from another AS:

  • Is the originating AS authorized? Does the first AS in the path have permission to advertise this destination?
  • Is the path valid? Are the ASes actually connected in the order listed?
  • Is the advertisement authorized? Does each AS along the path have permission to pass the route forward?
  • Will traffic follow the advertised path? When routers forward packets using this route, will they actually traverse the AS path shown?

These four questions set the stage for the rest of the analysis. Each one sounds straightforward, but the document shows that answering them is far more complex than it initially appears in real, deployed networks.
sections.eli5: When someone tells you how to get somewhere, you might ask: Did they start from the right place? Is the route actually possible? Are all the stops along the way letting people through? Will following the instructions actually work?

sections.title: Forwarding Consistency is Not Guaranteed
sections.content:
The RFC presents four detailed examples that illustrate problems in deployed networks. The first example shows how manual routing policy within an AS can cause traffic to take a different path than the one advertised in BGP.

Consider a network where AS65000 advertises a route to AS65001, claiming the path goes through AS65002. However, a network administrator in AS65001 might have configured a static route that directs traffic through a different path. The result: the BGP announcement says one thing, but traffic forwarded according to that announcement takes a different route.

This leads to a crucial realization: since each router makes independent forwarding decisions based on its local routing table, traffic can be redirected at any hop. An upstream router cannot know in advance what path traffic will actually take. Therefore, forwarding consistency (the property that traffic follows the advertised AS path) cannot be validated in a deployed network.
sections.eli5: Imagine telling someone: 'Take Main Street, then Oak Avenue.' But when they reach Oak Avenue, the road is blocked, so they take Elm Street instead. There is no way for you to have known that ahead of time.

sections.title: Three Types of Authorization in Conflict
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three different meanings of 'authorization' in routing, and shows they often conflict:

  • Route authorization: Does AS X have permission to advertise this specific prefix?
  • Destination authorization: Does AS X have permission to advertise all destinations within this prefix (including more-specific subprefixes)?
  • Transit authorization: Does AS X have permission to forward traffic to all destinations within this prefix?

In routing systems, these three concepts are tightly intertwined. When an AS advertises a route (say, 10.0.0.0/16), the receiving routers implicitly assume the advertising AS is authorized for both destination and transit within that prefix. But in real networks, this assumption often does not hold. For example, an AS might be authorized to advertise 10.0.0.0/16 but not to advertise or transit to 10.1.1.0/24, a subblock that is actually allocated to a different party.

The RFC demonstrates through examples that simply proving route authorization does not prove destination or transit authorization. Yet routing systems cannot easily separate these concepts without losing efficiency and scalability.
sections.eli5: Imagine a warehouse manager authorized to deliver packages to Building A. But the warehouse manager assumes this authorization also covers small offices inside Building A, which actually have their own rules about who can deliver there. These three authorizations (overall, specific location, and actual traffic rights) are tangled together.

sections.title: Route Aggregation Creates Hidden Paths
sections.content:
One of the clearest examples in the RFC involves route aggregation. Imagine AS65000 does not want a specific prefix (10.1.1.0/24) to be advertised beyond AS65001. It adds a BGP NO_ADVERTISE community to prevent readvertisement. However, AS65001 might advertise a default route (0.0.0.0/0) to downstream networks. When traffic destined to 10.1.1.0/24 arrives at AS65002, it might follow the default route and eventually reach 10.1.1.0/24 anyway, bypassing the original policy.

The RFC points out that once a route is aggregated, information about more-specific prefixes is lost. An AS cannot verify the authorization for subblocks within an aggregate. The routing system has no way to know all the suballocations and authorization rules for every possible subprefix. This exposes a fundamental tension: aggregation is necessary for routing scalability, but it also prevents fine-grained authorization checks.
sections.eli5: Imagine a mailroom rule that says 'Don't deliver to Office B.' But the mailroom also delivers to 'Main Building,' which contains Office B. Someone looking only at the 'Main Building' delivery might deliver to Office B by accident.

sections.title: Implications and Limitations
sections.content:
RFC 5123 does not propose solutions; instead, it establishes why the problem is structural. The AS path is fundamentally designed to prevent routing loops (by showing each AS only once), not to provide security or path verification. Using the AS path for authorization or security purposes conflicts with the way routing actually works.

The document concludes that route authorization, destination authorization, and transit authorization cannot be easily separated in a deployed routing system without significantly reducing scalability. There are no easy or obviously scalable solutions. The RFC recommends that anyone evaluating path validation schemes understand these fundamental limitations before deciding whether a proposed solution is practical for real networks.
sections.eli5: The core lesson is that a list of stops in a message is designed to prevent the message from going in circles, not to guarantee it takes a particular route or that the right people touched it.
